abstract: Advances in artificial metalloenzyme design have expanded the range of reactions accessible to enzymes, yet the diversity of available scaffolds remains limited. Experimental activity data for individual non-native reactions are scarce, making it difficult to establish how the environment around a metal center shapes catalysis across scaffolds. Using phenylsilane-driven asymmetric reduction of acetophenone as a model reaction, we developed a workflow that combines structure-guided mining, experimental activity assays, and small-sample machine learning. We used the Zn-His coordination motif to mine experimental Protein Data Bank structures and AlphaFold predictions and grouped 2,660 candidate sequences into 200 structural clusters. Of 25 samples assayed, eight met the 10% apparent-yield threshold, including the positive enzymatic control. To evaluate small-sample learning, we assembled literature-derived training sets that differed in scaffold diversity. Training on the larger, more diverse dataset substantially improved recall on the experimental test set. Feature ablation identified contributions from pocket and tunnel geometry, hydrophobicity and solvent exposure, and local packing and metal coordination. These results provide a basis for discovering natural enzyme scaffolds with non-native activities from structural data.
